name: angelsea (MIR-based AngelScript JIT)
baseline: AngelScript interpreter (stock bytecode VM, JIT instructions off); also BlindMindStudios AngelScript JIT
workload: README: a 1 million iteration loop of AngelScript calls into a registered native function using the generic calling convention (tests/scripts/abi.as benchmark_1M_calls_noarg and benchmark_1M_calls_method_arg), JIT versus the interpreter in the same engine; separately an unpublished real-world game (King Arthur's Gold dev build) versus the BlindMindStudios JIT.
claimed_speedup: README: 'This allows angelsea to give a ~5x performance uplift for a 1 million generic calls benchmark' (vs the AngelScript interpreter); 'Compared to the BlindMindStudios JIT, we obtain +0~40% runtime performance in a real world application, but YMMV.'
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the benchmark; README build instructions say cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release; JIT backend is MIR via c2mir with mir_optimization_level 2 (default); test JitConfig uses eager compilation and experimental_stack_elision.
stars_or_usage: 31 stars; used in a King Arthur's Gold dev build per README
tradeoffs: Alpha quality per README. Needs AngelScript 2.37.0+ (asIJITCompilerV2), a downstream MIR fork and fmt; x86-64 and (experimental) aarch64 only, no 32-bit x86 (use the BMS JIT there); macOS x86-64 fails CI. Not thread-safe across multithreaded contexts. Higher JIT compile time and memory use than the BMS JIT (README), mitigated by lazy compilation, async compile callback and skipping huge functions. Bytecode is translated to C, then c2mir to machine code.
caveats: Both headline numbers are first-party and thin. The 5x figure is JIT versus the stock interpreter on a calls-only micro benchmark (empty native function via a hacked asCGeneric path, 1M iterations), not versus the BMS JIT; the repo prints nanobench output but commits no results and states no CPU or compiler flags. The 0-40% versus BMS JIT figure is from a private real-world application with no published script, data or hardware (README: 'YMMV. If you have results to share, we're interested!'). The repo also carries a brainfuck-interpreter benchmark (tests/megatests.cpp) with no published numbers. Last commit is just over 12 months old, so maintenance is stale.

name: Box86 (x86 userspace emulator for ARM with dynarec)
baseline: QEMU user-mode (x86 guest) and FEX; also Box86's own interpreter
workload: box86.org article 'Box86/Box64 vs QEMU vs FEX (vs Rosetta2)' (March 2022, by the Box86/Box64 author): 7-Zip benchmark MIPS run as an x86 (32-bit) guest under QEMU user-mode, FEX and Box86 on an ARM Linux machine, against the same benchmark built natively for ARM; further rows for dav1d and glmark2.
claimed_speedup: Search-result text of the article: 7-Zip MIPS native ARM 6157, Box86 3117 (about 50% of native), FEX 1197 (about 19%), QEMU 691 (about 11%), so Box86 is about 4.5x QEMU and about 2.6x FEX (derived from page data); glmark2 Box86 178 versus native 181. Repo docs/README.md: 'DynaRec ... providing a speed boost between 5 to 10 times faster than only using the interpreter.'
tradeoffs: Needs a 32-bit ARM userspace (armhf, a multiarch or chroot environment on aarch64) and is useless on 64-bit-only systems; runs x86 Linux programs only (x86_64 is the separate Box64 project, already catalogued from the same article); wraps native system libraries (libc, libm, SDL, OpenGL), which is where much of the speed on games comes from; dynarec uses memory protection plus a SIGSEGV handler, so debugging JIT-using programs under gdb is noisy.
caveats: Snippet only: box86.org is blocked here (EGRESS_BLOCKED), so the article itself was not opened and the numbers come from WebSearch result text, which gave the 7-Zip and glmark2 rows but no CPU model, compiler flags, guest binary versions or QEMU and FEX versions. The measurement is from March 2022 and was made by the Box86 author, a competing project; FEX has changed substantially since (per the catalogued FEX entry, a FEX maintainer said in October 2024 that he had never compared FEX with Box). The same article's Box64 and Rosetta2 comparison ran on an Apple M1; the machine for the Box86 rows is not visible. glmark2 and game rows mostly measure native GL pass-through, not the JIT. The 5-10x dynarec claim in the README is versus Box86's own interpreter and has no workload, CPU or flags. The article is also the source used for the catalogued Box64 and FEX entries.

Gist total runtime: C++ 0.72 s, Java 0.81, JavaScript 0.96, HashLink 5.68, Neko 27.16, PHP 12.59, Python 48.73, Lua 60.55, so hxcpp is about 7.9x faster than HashLink and about 38x faster than Neko (derived from page data). September 2025 rerun (runtime seconds, cpp versus hl versus neko): Anonymous 0.1 / 0.19 / 2.68, BinaryTrees 0.05 / 0.32 / 1.42, Mandelbrot 0.13 / 1.32 / 8.83, NBodies 0.02 / 0.07 / 3.35, IntArray 0.01 / 0.03 / 3.07, Fib 0 / 0.04 / 0.58.

stars_or_usage: 329 stars; the C++ target of the Haxe compiler (3,138 commits)
tradeoffs: hxcpp is the runtime support for the Haxe C++ backend: Haxe source is compiled to C++ and then built by the platform C++ compiler, so builds are slow (about 2 s per small program in the gist versus 0.1 to 0.2 s for neko, hl, js) and need a C++ toolchain; it ships its own garbage collector and runtime library and has the cppia scripting host. Output is native code, so it is the fastest Haxe target on most of these rows but the language semantics follow Haxe, not C++.
caveats: The measurements are an individual's gist, not an official suite, and neither Haxe nor hxcpp versions, the C++ compiler or its flags are given, so the run is below tier A (the benchmark code is public in HaxeFoundation/hashlink other/benchs). Even against HashLink the win is not on every row: HL/JIT beat cpp on Anonymous in 2018 (0.29 s versus 0.38 s). Against the other baselines the win is not clear: the gist's 2018 totals put C++ 0.72 s next to Java 0.81 and JavaScript 0.96, and in the 2025 rows JVM and Node are faster than cpp on several rows (Anonymous 0.03 and 0.02 versus 0.1, BinaryTrees 0.02 versus 0.05, Mandelbrot 0.07 versus 0.13; derived from page data), while many cells are rounded to 0.01 s so small ratios are unreliable. The hxcpp LICENSE.txt is a one-condition BSD notice ('See individual source files for additional license information'), so bundled third-party code carries its own terms.

name: FAFO (parallel EVM transaction scheduler on revm)
baseline: state-of-the-art sharded execution (paper's cost baseline); no sequential revm or pevm comparison found
workload: bench-sendeth: replay of native ETH and ERC-20 transfer workloads (zero contention 'none', hot-account 'hotn', and replayed real-trace generators) over a 2^30-account QMDB database with Merkleization every block, using revm for execution on one many-core node; the README claims throughput scaling and a cost comparison.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Over 1 million Merkleized EVM-Compatible transactions per second while maintaining state verifiability'; 'Near-linear throughput scaling up to 96 cores and beyond on a single machine'; '91% cheaper than sharded execution'. Search-result text of the paper (arXiv 2507.10757): over 1.1 million native ETH transfers per second and over half a million ERC-20 transfers per second on a single node. No timing of sequential revm or pevm on the same workload is given in the repo.
compiler_and_flags: Rust toolchain pinned by rust-toolchain.toml; benchmark run with cargo run --release through bench-sendeth/run.sh; revm 20.0.0 and alloy 0.11.1 per workspace Cargo.toml.
hardware: Repo states none. Third-party article snippet (OAK Research, not opened): one AWS server with 96 vCPUs, 786 GiB DRAM and six NVMe SSDs in RAID0 (22.5 TB).
tradeoffs: A transaction scheduler and pipeline (ParaLyze address estimation, ParaFramer with ParaBloom Bloom filters to group non-conflicting transactions into frames, ParaScheduler precedence graphs) rather than a new EVM interpreter: it runs revm and QMDB underneath, so gains come from parallel scheduling of independent transfers and are bounded by contention. Needs a very large machine (the benchmark initialises a database with billions of accounts, and the README's Docker setup asks for at least 256 GB of virtual disk and 32 GB of memory). Synthetic transfer workloads; the repo is described as ongoing research.
caveats: Not a faster-than-baseline claim in the sense of the listed baselines: neither the README nor bench-sendeth compares against sequential revm or pevm on a common workload (the only comparison in the README is '91% cheaper than sharded execution', a cost figure against a non-named baseline, with the methodology in a paper that is blocked here: layerzero.network and arxiv.org returned EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the paper's numbers come from search-result text only). The workloads are plain ETH and ERC-20 transfers, which is far easier to parallelise than general contract code; the paper is 'Under submission' (not peer reviewed). The repo holds a single 'Initial commit' dated 2025-06-26, so there is no development history to check, and the 96-vCPU machine is only known from a third-party article snippet. pevm and revm are catalogued separately, and Block-STM style comparison, if any, is in the unopened paper.

name: evm.zig (evmz, Zig EVM execution engine)
baseline: evmone (v0.23.0, baseline and advanced interpreters) and revm (=43.0.2 raw interpreter, Interpreter::run_plain)
workload: VM-core 'compare' lane over the evm-bench-style fixtures (arithmetic loop, MSTORE loop, keccak loop, ten-thousand-hashes, SLOAD and SSTORE loops, LOG0/LOG4 with 0 and 32 byte data, ERC20 mint, transfer and approval+transfer, snailtracer): deployed runtime bytecode called repeatedly through each engine's interpreter-level path with analysis prepared outside the timed window, fixed Osaka spec, median of 100-run medians, lower time is better.
claimed_speedup: README (Apple M1 Max, ReleaseFast, 2026-08-13), evmz versus evmone-base versus revm-int: Arithmetic loop 0.104 / 0.109 / 0.501 ms, Storage SSTORE loop 0.162 / 0.854 / 0.875 ms, ERC20 transfer 3.761 / 6.247 / 6.084 ms, Snailtracer 19.965 / 59.804 / 37.990 ms. bench/README.md ratios (base/evmz and revm/evmz): SSTORE 5.27x and 5.40x, SLOAD 3.97x and 2.34x, snailtracer 3.00x and 1.90x, ERC20 transfer 1.66x and 1.62x, Arithmetic 1.05x and 4.82x. evmz is slower than evmone-base on MSTORE loop (0.125 vs 0.084 ms, 0.67x), LOG0 32-byte (0.057 vs 0.033 ms, 0.58x), LOG0 0-byte (0.69x), LOG4 0-byte (0.80x) and ten-thousand-hashes (0.86x). AMD EPYC Genoa (KVM guest pinned to one CPU) rows are near parity with evmone-base: ERC20 transfer 7.686 vs 7.447 ms (0.97x), arithmetic 0.151 vs 0.145 ms (0.96x), keccak loop 4.597 vs 4.584 ms (1.00x), snailtracer 33.347 vs 57.983 ms (1.74x), SSTORE 0.595 vs 0.838 ms (1.41x), and ahead of revm on every row (1.08x to 3.08x).
compiler_and_flags: Zig >= 0.16.0, zig build bench-compare -Dbench-optimize=ReleaseFast -Dbench-support-min=osaka -Dbench-support-max=osaka -Dnative-keccak=xkcp -- --spec osaka --num-runs 100 --warmup-ms 100 (five repeats, median); all engines built without frame pointers (evmone via -fomit-frame-pointer inside the Zig build, evmone v0.23.0 with intx 0.15.0); revm 43.0.2 built with Cargo --release, RUSTFLAGS=-C target-cpu=native -C force-frame-pointers=no, fat LTO, one codegen unit.
hardware: Apple M1 Max, macOS arm64 (headline snapshot, 2026-08-13); AMD EPYC Genoa, Linux x86-64, KVM guest pinned to one CPU (earlier snapshot).
tradeoffs: Tail-call-dispatch interpreter in Zig with fork rules, tracing and single-step selected at compile time (separate binaries), zero-alloc pooled executor, optional XKCP Keccak and native crypto libraries (blst, mcl, libsecp256k1) as lazy dependencies, zkVM guest builds (ZisK, SP1, OpenVM). The headline numbers enable the optional XKCP Keccak provider ('maximum-performance configuration'). Pre-1.0 (version 0.0.0), builds need a very recent Zig (0.16).
caveats: Comparison is VM-core only: interpreter execute() with analysis prepared outside the timed window, no transaction validation, journal or database, so it is not a whole-client comparison (the repo says the executor lane is deliberately later). Correctness check in all three runners is limited to a success status (evmz result.status() == success, evmone EVMC_SUCCESS, revm result.is_ok()); the compare lane does not assert that return data, gas used or log counts match across engines (it only records host call counts). The README headline table shows the four rows where evmz wins; the full M1 table also has rows where evmone-baseline is faster (MSTORE loop, LOG0 and LOG4 rows, ten-thousand-hashes), and on the AMD snapshot evmz is within about 7% of evmone-base on 9 of 14 rows (ratios 0.94x to 1.07x, derived from page data) and slower on the LOG0 rows (0.73x, 0.75x). The AMD snapshot is older and run in a KVM guest. Revm is timed through its raw interpreter, not a transaction path. The repo contains CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md (AI-assisted development); first-party numbers only, 3 stars. Not the cryptuon/zig-evm project, which is rejected for a hard-coded table.

name: Cuik (C compiler with the TB backend)
baseline: clang 22.1.8 (LLVM) and gcc 16.2.1 / gcc-15 15.3.0, compile and build time at their default optimisation level
workload: nordlow/compiler-benchmark generates a synthetic C program (a grid of nested function call chains, 'return expr' bodies, long type) and measures minimum time per generated function over 5 runs for the check (syntax-only), compile (-c) and build (link to an executable) operations; Cuik is capped at 100 x 100 functions, the other C compilers run 200 x 200.
claimed_speedup: README sample run (us per generated function, lower is better), Cuik versus clang 22.1.8 versus gcc 16.2.1: check 6.0 / 15.4 / 18.2, compile 60.6 / 123.3 / 732.5, build 57.6 / 60.3 / 500.7. That is Cuik about 2.0x faster than clang and about 12x faster than gcc at compile, about 2.6x and 3.0x at check, and about 1.05x and 8.7x at build (all derived from page data). tcc 0.9.28rc is faster again (check 2.9, compile 3.5, build 2.6) and cproc is slower (check 10.6, compile 114.8). README conclusion: 'TCC is by a large margin the fastest compiler in build speed, followed by the C compiler Cuik and D's dmd.'
compiler_and_flags: Cuik ~master (no commit given) invoked with -c -xe (check), -c (compile) and plain -o exe (build); clang 22.1.8 and gcc 16.2.1 invoked with -fsyntax-only, -c and plain build with no -O flag (so their default O0 code generation) plus warning-silencing flags, from the benchmark script.
hardware: AMD Ryzen AI 7 350 (8+8) @ 5.09 GHz, Arch Linux, sample run as of 2026-09
tradeoffs: Cuik's own README: 'warning: unfinished and buggy'. Fast, thread-safe C11 front end (libCuik) plus the Tilde Backend (tb) with a sea-of-nodes IR, x64 and AArch64 codegen, ELF, COFF, PE and Mach-O output, and JIT or AOT use; MIT licensed. In the benchmark Cuik's build peak memory is far higher per function (69.9 kB/f versus clang 8.8 and gcc 17.5) and the benchmark had to cap Cuik at 100 x 100 for 'compiler stability limits'. No optimising pipeline comparable to LLVM, so it competes on compile speed rather than code quality.
caveats: Independent third-party suite, but the gap to tier A is the Cuik build: it is labelled '~master' with no commit or build flags, and results are from one sample run on one machine (best of 5 per cell). The comparison is at default (effectively -O0) settings for clang and gcc, on one synthetic program shape (long nested one-line functions), so it measures front end plus unoptimised codegen speed only; the 'Run' column (105 us/f for Cuik versus 155 clang and 98 gcc) is of unoptimised output on a synthetic program and says nothing about code quality, which the lead named as a baseline and for which no numbers were found. Numbers are normalised per function while Cuik runs a smaller 10,000-function program than the others (40,000 functions), so fixed start-up cost weighs more on Cuik, which if anything understates its speed. Cuik's repo and docs themselves carry no benchmark, and a search-result snippet saying its preprocessor is about 2x faster than Clang's was not verified. LLVM as a library (TB versus LLVM backend) is not measured here.

name: LC Scheme BBV JIT (bsaleil/lc)
baseline: Gambit Scheme (gsc) and Chez Scheme; the repo harness compares against both but commits no results
workload: JIT compiler for Scheme on Linux x86-64 using lazy basic-block versioning with interprocedural code versioning; the README example runs fib(40) and prints the time, and tools/benchtimes/run.py plus tools/ecoop17-paper.sh reproduce the ECOOP'17 experiments over the classic Gambit benchmark set (ack, boyer, browse, compiler, conform, cpstak, deriv, earley, fft, fib, mbrot, nbody, nqueens, nucleic, peval, sum, tak, takl and others).
claimed_speedup: No numeric comparison against Gambit, Chez Scheme or any other baseline appears in the repo. README: 'time ./lc fib.scm' for fib(40) = 165580141, real 0.550 s, user 0.537 s, with no baseline. Search-result text of the ECOOP 2017 paper abstract says the technique removes almost all run-time type checks for several benchmarks, 'allowing the compiler to generate code up to 50% faster' (baseline not stated in the snippet; the paper itself was not opened).
stars_or_usage: 33 stars; three peer-reviewed papers (SFPW 2014, SFPW 2015, ECOOP 2017)
tradeoffs: Research JIT, Linux x86-64 only, written in Gambit Scheme and needs a modified Gambit (bsaleil/gambit) fork built first and gsc on PATH at build and run time; the build target is 'make debug'. The repo carries the benchmark harness (tools/benchtimes/run.py defines Gambit, Chez Scheme, Pycket and several LC configurations, with hard-coded author paths and most systems commented out) and benchmark sources under tools/benchtimes/resultVMIL-lc-gsc-lc, but those directories hold preprocessed benchmark programs, not timing results. The fib(40) example is a demo with no comparison. Last commit 2019-05-11, so the project is abandoned.
